findings.title: Double free / use-after-free in IntoIter::drop when an element's Drop panics
findings.evidence: Reachable from 100% safe code. `IntoIter::drop` (lines 2539-2556) calls the nested `drop_non_singleton` (2544-2550): it moves the backing `ThinVec` out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` (2546), then destroys the not-yet-yielded elements with `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (2547), and only afterwards does `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (2548). If any element's `Drop` panics (panic=unwind, the default), line 2548 never executes and the local `vec` is dropped during unwinding with its length still equal to the full original length; `ThinVec::drop` (1910-1930) then runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (1917) over 0..len, (a) re-dropping elements [start, panic_idx) that were already destroyed by the panicked drop_in_place (double free) and (b) dropping elements [0, start) that `Iterator::next` (2503-2513) already moved out via `ptr::read` and that the caller still owns (use-after-free / double drop of live values). Trigger: `let v = thin_vec![String::from("a"), PanicOnDrop(...), ...]; let it = v.into_iter(); drop(it);` where a remaining element's Drop panics. This is RUSTSEC-2026-0103 / CVE-2026-6654 / GHSA-xphw-cqx3-667j (thin-vec < 0.2.16; this tree claims 0.2.15). The std fix pattern (set the length to 0 via a drop guard/zeroing BEFORE the element drop) is absent here; e.g. `truncate` at 1055-1066 in this same file does order `set_len` before `drop_in_place`, confirming the ordering here is the defect, not intended behavior. Impact: heap double free reachable from safe Rust, exploitable for memory corruption (the advisory documents an ACE primitive via vtable hijacking).

findings.title: Double free in ThinVec::clear when an element's Drop panics
findings.evidence: Reachable from 100% safe code. `ThinVec::clear` (lines 1082-1087) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (1084) BEFORE `self.set_len(0)` (1085). If an element's `Drop` panics mid-clear (panic=unwind), `set_len(0)` is skipped and the `ThinVec` still reports its old length; when it is subsequently dropped (the normal case: it is a local variable, so it is dropped while the panic unwinds), `ThinVec::drop` (1910-1930) executes `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (1917) over 0..old_len, re-dropping the elements [0, panic_idx) that were already destroyed (double free). Trigger: `let mut v = thin_vec![String::from("x"), DropsPanic, ...]; v.clear();` The std-equivalent implementation avoids this by being `self.truncate(0)`, and this file's own `truncate` (1055-1066) correctly decrements the length before each `drop_in_place`, confirming the ordering in `clear` is a defect. Advisory reference: RUSTSEC-2026-0103 / CVE-2026-6654 (thin-vec < 0.2.16; this tree claims 0.2.15). Impact: heap double free from safe Rust, memory corruption.
